attacks.area: Requests a web page could make
attacks.attack: A web page posts a command as text/plain, the one body type browsers send to other sites without a preflight check.
attacks.defence: Bodies must be application/rayfold+json, application/json or application/rayfold; anything else gets 415 before parsing.
attacks.guard: The same command sent as application/rayfold+json runs.

response.body: {"type":"https://eddyboutros.github.io/rayfold/errors/unsupported_media_type","title":"unsupported media type","status":415,"detail":"Content-Type text/plain is not accepted; send application/rayfold+json","code":"invalid_argument"}

attacks.area: Requests a web page could make
attacks.attack: A page on another site sends a JSON command with the user's credentials.
attacks.defence: Requests that change data and carry an Origin must come from the server's own origin or an allowed one; others get 403.
attacks.guard: The same request from the server's own origin runs.

attacks.area: Requests a web page could make
attacks.attack: An HTML form on another site posts to POST /orders/{id}/pay, a route with no body.
attacks.defence: The Origin check covers the REST-style routes too, and POST routes also require an Idempotency-Key header, which a form cannot set.
attacks.guard: The same POST from an app, with its Idempotency-Key, pays the order.

attacks.area: Requests a web page could make
attacks.attack: A page renames its own domain to 127.0.0.1 (DNS rebinding) to talk to a server on the user's machine as if it were the same site.
attacks.defence: A server reached on a loopback address answers only loopback host names (localhost, 127.0.0.1, [::1]); other Host headers get 403.
attacks.guard: The same request with Host 127.0.0.1 is answered.

response.body: {"type":"https://eddyboutros.github.io/rayfold/errors/permission_denied","title":"permission denied","status":403,"detail":"Host evil.example:57322 is not allowed on a loopback server","code":"permission_denied"}

attacks.area: Requests a web page could make
attacks.attack: A web page sends tools/call to the MCP endpoint of a Rayfold server on the user's machine or intranet.
attacks.defence: MCP requests with a foreign Origin get 403, as the MCP specification requires, and loopback servers check the Host header.
attacks.guard: An AI client (no browser Origin) lists and calls tools.

attacks.area: Requests a web page could make
attacks.attack: A page sends MCP JSON-RPC as text/plain to avoid the browser's preflight check.
attacks.defence: The MCP endpoint accepts only application/json (415 otherwise).
attacks.guard: tools/list as application/json is answered.

response.body: {"type":"https://eddyboutros.github.io/rayfold/errors/unsupported_media_type","title":"unsupported media type","status":415,"detail":"Content-Type text/plain is not accepted; send application/json","code":"invalid_argument"}

attacks.area: Requests a web page could make
attacks.attack: A page on another site opens a WebSocket to Rayfold; the browser attaches the user's cookies to the handshake.
attacks.defence: The handshake is refused with 403 unless the Origin is the server's own or allowed (and the Host is valid).
attacks.guard: A client without a foreign Origin gets 101 Switching Protocols.

attacks.attack: A request nests its arguments 10,000 levels deep to exhaust the server's stack.
attacks.defence: Arguments and variables deeper than 64 levels fail the batch with invalid_argument, checked without recursion.
attacks.guard: A normal request is answered.

attacks.attack: A shape nested 5,000 levels deep, to make the parser recurse until it crashes.
attacks.defence: The shape parser stops at 64 levels of nesting and answers invalid_argument; execution depth is capped separately (8 by default).
attacks.guard: A shape nested a few levels runs.

attacks.attack: Three expensive list queries plus a fourth with a page size of -100,000, hoping the negative size cancels out their cost.
attacks.defence: An op with invalid arguments never runs and costs 0; untrusted page sizes count as the largest page; every op costs at least 1.
attacks.guard: One of the expensive queries alone fits the budget and runs.

request.body: {"ops":[{"id":1,"op":"books","args":{"page":{"first":200}},"shape":"{ items { id title author { name } } }"},{"id":2,"op":"books","args":{"page":{"first":200}},"shape":"{ items { id title author { name } } }"},{"id":3,"op":"books","args":{"page":{"first":200}},"shape":"{ items { id title author { name } } }"},{"id":4,"op":"books","args":{"page":{"first":-100000}}}]}

attacks.attack: A 1.5 MB request body, to make the server buffer and parse huge input.
attacks.defence: Bodies over the limit (1 MiB by default) get 413 Content Too Large; the rest of the upload is drained up to a bound, then the connection is cut.
attacks.guard: A normal body is answered.

attacks.attack: A WebSocket client announces a 2 MiB frame and keeps streaming, to fill the server's memory.
attacks.defence: Frames and assembled messages over 1 MiB close the connection with code 1009 (message too big).
attacks.guard: A normal message on a new socket is answered.

request.body: text frame announcing 2,097,152 bytes, then 1.2 MB of data

attacks.attack: A client sends thousands of distinct inline shapes; each one used to be remembered forever.
attacks.defence: Shapes learned from requests are kept up to a limit (10,000 by default; 10 in this test), least recently used first out; rejected shapes are never kept.
attacks.guard: Shapes registered by the server itself stay, and every request is still answered.

request.body: {"ops":[{"id":1,"op":"book","args":{"id":"b1"},"shape":"{ id format price stock alias29: title }"}]}

attacks.attack: A client sends thousands of commands with new idempotency keys; the records used to be kept until someone read them again.
attacks.defence: Records expire (24 hours by default), expired ones are swept on every write, and past a size limit (100,000 by default; 10 here) the oldest go first.
attacks.guard: The most recent key still replays its result.

attacks.attack: A client sends a negative or enormous deadline.
attacks.defence: Deadlines must be whole milliseconds from 0 to 600,000; anything else is invalid_argument.
attacks.guard: A 5,000 ms deadline is honoured.

attacks.attack: A client reuses the key of a paid order's payOrder call on cancelOrder, so the cancel is answered with the stored payment result and never runs.
attacks.defence: A key is bound to its operation and arguments; reusing it for anything else is already_exists, and the write policy is checked before any replay.
attacks.guard: Retrying payOrder with its own key replays the payment.

response.body: {"id":1,"error":{"code":"already_exists","message":"Idempotency key attack-key-0000000001 was used for another operation or other arguments"},"fin":true}

attacks.attack: An app on a flaky network sends the same order twice at the same moment; both copies used to run.
attacks.defence: The first request claims the key; the second waits for it to finish and replays its result.
attacks.guard: Both requests get the same order back.

attacks.attack: Every anonymous caller shares one replay scope, so one guest could replay another guest's result, or probe which keys exist.
attacks.defence: A command with an idempotency key needs an identified caller (a user, service or guest session); anonymous keyed commands are unauthenticated.
attacks.guard: An identified caller's retry replays its own result.

attacks.attack: A customer asks for other customers' order ids with an explicit shape, to learn which orders exist.
attacks.defence: A denied entity at a nullable position reads as null even with an explicit shape, so forbidden and missing look the same.
attacks.guard: The owner gets the order.

attacks.attack: An anonymous caller downloads the manifest to read every permission rule, such as who may see costPrice.
attacks.defence: The manifest keeps names and types but removes policy expressions; the full schema is opt-in, and the manifest can be switched off.
attacks.guard: Clients still get every type and operation they need.

attacks.attack: A batch points $ref at "1.constructor" or "1.__proto__" to pull built-in objects into the arguments.
attacks.defence: $ref paths read only the earlier result's own data; anything else resolves to nothing.
attacks.guard: $ref to "1.id" passes the book's id along.

attacks.attack: A request carries a "__proto__" or "constructor" key in its arguments, beside a $ref or in a REST-style body, so the server's copy of the arguments would take attacker data as its prototype and pass on values validation never saw.
attacks.defence: Arguments are copied key by key as plain data, the way JSON.parse reads them, so the key fails validation as an unknown argument and nothing reaches Object.prototype.
attacks.guard: The same requests without the extra key are served, with the filter and page size they really carry.

attacks.attack: A binary (RB) request carries an argument object whose key is "__proto__", so decoding it would swap the object's prototype and smuggle in arguments.
attacks.defence: The decoder stores every key as plain data, so the request fails validation as an unknown argument.
attacks.guard: A normal binary request is answered.

attacks.attack: An AI agent asks for a dry run of a command whose code forgets to check ctx.simulate, so the "dry run" would really write.
attacks.defence: Only commands that declare @simulate accept dry runs, and only they get a .simulate tool in MCP; others answer failed_precondition.
attacks.guard: Declared commands, such as placeOrder, still offer a dry run that writes nothing.

attacks.attack: A rule denies payments over 1000, but Decimal amounts travel as text, and text compared with a number used to count as "not greater".
attacks.defence: Numbers and numeric text compare exactly by value (also beyond 2^53), and a rule that cannot be evaluated fails closed.
attacks.guard: An amount of 999.99 is allowed.

attacks.attack: A client sends the id 9007199254740993 as a JSON number, which JavaScript silently rounds to a different id.
attacks.defence: Integers beyond 2^53 and Decimals written in exponent form are refused; send them as text.
attacks.guard: The same id as text is accepted.

attacks.attack: A browser second-guesses a response's type (MIME sniffing) and runs data as a script, or a shared cache keeps an error page.
attacks.defence: Every response carries X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and refusals carry Cache-Control: no-store.
attacks.guard: Responses keep their declared content types, and 304 answers stay minimal.

response.body: {"type":"https://eddyboutros.github.io/rayfold/errors/unsupported_media_type","title":"unsupported media type","status":415,"detail":"Content-Type text/plain is not accepted; send application/rayfold+json","code":"invalid_argument"}

attacks.attack: A client opens a WebSocket, starts a live query, then vanishes without a close frame, so the server would keep the socket and the subscription forever.
attacks.defence: The server closes its side as soon as the client's side ends, which cancels that connection's live queries.
attacks.guard: While the connection is open, its live query stays subscribed.
